abstract.t: OpenID Connect 1.0 has become a popular choice for single sign-on in enterprise use cases. To improve interoperability, OpenID Connect Enterprise Extensions specifies a number of common or desirable extensions to OpenID Connect.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: OpenID Connect 1.0 is a widely adopted identity protocol that enables client applications, known as relying parties (RPs), to verify the identity of end-users based on authentication performed by a trusted service, the OpenID Provider (OP).

Initial adoption of OpenID Connect was by sites providing personal identity to applications. OpenID Connect has become a popular choice in enterprise use cases, and implementors have defined their own extensions for use cases that were not addressed in the original specification.

To improve interoperability between systems, OpenID Connect Enterprise Extensions specifies optional claims that may be included in an ID Token, optional parameters that may be included in an authentication request, optional client registration parameters, and optional parameters that may be included when initiating login from a third party.

Enterprise deployments are often multi-tenant on both sides of the protocol: an OP may serve many organizations, and an RP may be a SaaS application serving many customer organizations. OpenID Connect Core names the OP with iss, the Account at the OP with sub, and the RP with aud. The extensions in this specification name what is left: the OP Tenant with the tenant claim, the RP Tenant with the aud_tenant claim, and the Account at the RP with the aud_sub claim. Appendix A describes the tenancy models these extensions serve, and is non-normative.

section.name: Requirements Notation and Conventions
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in RFC2119.

In the .txt version of this specification, values are quoted to indicate that they are to be taken literally. When using these values in protocol messages, the quotes MUST NOT be used as part of the value. In the HTML version of this specification, values to be taken literally are indicated by the use of this fixed-width font.

section.name: Terminology
section.t: This specification defines the following terms:

li.t: Account: A set of claims about a user.

Tenant: A logically isolated entity that represents a distinct organizational or administrative boundary. A Tenant may contain Accounts managed by individuals, or may contain Accounts managed by an organization.
OP Tenant: A Tenant within an OP. An OP may have a single Tenant, or multiple Tenants.
RP Tenant: A Tenant within an RP. An RP may have a single Tenant, or multiple Tenants.

section.name: ID Token Claims
section.t: An ID Token is defined in Section 2 of OpenID Connect Core 1.0.
Following are OPTIONAL claims that may be included in an ID Token:

section.name: session_expiry
section.t: The session_expiry claim is a JSON integer that represents the Unix timestamp (seconds since epoch) indicating when a session created from the ID Token MUST expire.

section.name: tenant
section.t: The tenant claim is a JSON string that identifies the OP Tenant the user authenticated to. The value MUST be personal, organization, or a tenant identifier that is stable, unique within the issuer, and opaque to the RP. The personal value is reserved for when Accounts are managed by individuals. The organization value is reserved for Accounts managed by an organization.
An OP that uses a distinct issuer identifier per OP Tenant SHOULD omit the tenant claim, as iss identifies the OP Tenant. If the claim is included, the value MUST be personal or organization.
An OP that uses a single issuer identifier for multiple OP Tenants SHOULD include the tenant claim. The value MUST be personal or a tenant identifier.

tr.td: Multiple Tenants, issuer identifier per Tenant

section.t: The tenant claim carries Tenant context; it does not participate in subject identifier uniqueness. Per Section 2 of OpenID Connect Core 1.0, the sub value MUST be unique within the issuer, which includes being unique across all OP Tenants sharing that issuer identifier.
An OP that includes the tenant claim SHOULD list tenant in the claims_supported metadata parameter defined in OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0.

section.name: aud_sub
section.t: The aud_sub claim is an opaque JSON string that represents the identifier the RP has for the Account. How the OP acquires the aud_sub, and how the OP Account and RP Account are linked, is out of scope of this specification.
The aud_sub value MUST be unique within the aud, which includes being unique across all RP Tenants sharing that client_id.

section.name: aud_tenant
section.t: The aud_tenant claim is a JSON string that identifies the RP Tenant the authentication was for. The value MUST be stable and unique within the aud, and is opaque to the OP.

If the RP provided the client_tenant authentication request parameter, the OP MUST set aud_tenant to that value. If the OP determines the RP Tenant by other means, such as domain_hint, login_hint, a default for the client, or user selection, the OP SHOULD include the aud_tenant claim. If the OP does not know the RP Tenant, the OP MUST omit the aud_tenant claim.
The aud_tenant and aud_sub claims are independent; either, both, or neither may be present.

section.name: Authentication Request Parameters
section.t: An Authentication Request is defined in Section 3.1.2.1 of OpenID Connect Core 1.0.
Following are OPTIONAL parameters that may be included in an Authentication Request:

section.name: domain_hint
section.t: The domain_hint parameter provides a hint for the OP to determine which OP Tenant to present to the user to authenticate to, typically a domain name such as example.com. The parameter is a hint and is not guaranteed to identify a single OP Tenant.

section.name: tenant
section.t: The tenant identifier per the tenant claim for the OP Tenant that the RP would like the user to be authenticated to. Passing a tenant value of personal indicates the RP would like the user to use an Account managed by the user. Passing a tenant value of organization indicates the RP would like the user to use an Account managed by an organization.
If both the tenant and domain_hint parameters are present, the tenant parameter takes precedence.
If the tenant value does not match an OP Tenant, the OP SHOULD return an invalid_request error.

section.name: client_tenant
section.t: The client_tenant identifier per the aud_tenant claim for the RP Tenant that the Authentication Request is for. This parameter is used by an RP that shares a client_id across multiple RP Tenants.

An OP that supports the client_tenant parameter MUST return the value in the aud_tenant claim. An OP that does not support the client_tenant parameter MUST ignore it and MUST omit the aud_tenant claim.
If the client registered the tenants client registration parameter and the client_tenant value is not one of the registered values, the OP SHOULD return an invalid_request error.
The OP MUST treat the redirect_uri as opaque and MUST NOT determine an RP Tenant from it.

section.name: Client Registration Parameters
section.t: Client registration is defined in OpenID Connect Dynamic Client Registration 1.0.
Following are OPTIONAL parameters that may be included in client registration:

section.name: tenants
section.t: The tenants parameter is a JSON array of strings containing the RP Tenant identifiers the client may provide in the client_tenant authentication request parameter. Registering the tenants parameter indicates the RP is multi-tenant and shares the client_id across its Tenants.
An OP MAY use the registered values to validate the client_tenant parameter and to apply RP Tenant specific policy.

section.name: Login from a Third Party Parameters
section.t: Initiating a login from a third party and a login initiation endpoint are defined in Section 4 of OpenID Connect Core 1.0.
Following are OPTIONAL parameters that may be included in request to the login initiation endpoint:

section.name: client_id
section.t: The client_id value the RP should use when making the Authentication Request. This allows a multi-tenant application that hosts multiple tenants, each represented by a different client_id, to know which client_id to use.

section.name: domain_hint
section.t: The domain_hint value to be included in the Authentication Request.

section.name: tenant
section.t: The tenant value to be included in the Authentication Request.

section.name: client_tenant
section.t: The client_tenant value to be included in the Authentication Request.

section.name: Tenant Isolation
section.t: The tenant claim MUST reflect the OP Tenant the user authenticated to. A user who authenticated to one OP Tenant MUST NOT be able to obtain an ID Token carrying a different OP Tenant's identifier.

section.name: Subject Identifier Collision
section.t: An RP identifies an Account by iss and sub. An OP serving multiple OP Tenants from a single issuer identifier MUST NOT issue the same sub value to different users in different OP Tenants. Doing so would cause an RP to link two users as one. The tenant claim does not relax this requirement.

section.name: Client Tenant Validation
section.t: The client_tenant parameter is supplied by the RP in the Authentication Request. An OP that applies RP Tenant specific policy SHOULD validate the value against the client's registered tenants. Without validation, a request can name any RP Tenant and receive that Tenant's policy.

section.name: Tenant Claim Validation
section.t: An RP that expects the tenant claim MUST verify it is present, and, when the RP knows which OP Tenant it expects, that the value matches. An RP that does not validate the claim may link Accounts from different OP Tenants, or apply Tenant specific access control for the wrong Tenant.

section.name: aud_tenant Claim Validation
section.t: An RP that provided the client_tenant parameter MUST reject the ID Token if the aud_tenant claim is absent or has a different value. Without this check, a token obtained for one RP Tenant can be presented to another.

section.name: Account Linking
section.t: An RP MUST link Accounts using the full identifier: iss and sub for the OP Account, and aud and aud_sub for the RP Account. Linking on sub alone will merge users from different OPs or different OP Tenants.

section.name: Cross-Tenant Response Handling
section.t: A multi-tenant RP that routes responses using the state parameter, a cookie, or session context MUST verify that the Authentication Response is processed in the same RP Tenant context that made the request.

section.name: Enterprise Tenancy Models
section.t: This appendix is non-normative.

An enterprise single sign-on names six things: the OP, the Account at the OP, the OP Tenant, the RP, the Account at the RP, and the RP Tenant. OpenID Connect Core names the first, second, and fourth with iss, sub, and aud. This specification names the rest.
section.artwork:
OP RP iss: https://idp.example.com aud: rp-shared-abcde
┌─────────────┬─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┬─────────────┐ │ OP Tenant │ OP Tenant │ │ RP Tenant │ RP Tenant │ │ acme-corp │ widgets-inc │ │ acme │ widgets │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ sub:user123 │ sub:user456 │ │ aud_sub:a-1 │ aud_sub:w-1 │ │ sub:user124 │ sub:user457 │ │ aud_sub:a-2 │ aud_sub:w-2 │ └─────────────┴─────────────┘ └─────────────┴─────────────┘
the tenant claim names the aud_tenant claim names which column which column

section.name: An OP with many Tenants
section.t: An OP that serves many organizations has made one architectural choice before any RP arrives: whether each Tenant gets its own issuer identifier, or whether all Tenants share one.
An issuer identifier per Tenant. Each OP Tenant has its own issuer identifier, metadata document, and signing keys. Nothing further is needed, because iss names the Tenant.
The cost is borne by the RP: every Tenant is a separate OP to discover, configure, and trust.

One issuer identifier for all Tenants. All OP Tenants share one issuer identifier, one metadata document, and one set of signing keys. An RP configures the OP once and serves every Tenant. Since iss no longer names the Tenant, the OP names it in the tenant claim.

In both models sub is unique within iss, as OpenID Connect Core requires. Two users in two Tenants of the same issuer never share a sub. The tenant claim answers "which Tenant is this user in", not "which user is this".

tr.td: One issuer identifier, metadata document, and set of signing keys for all Tenants
Multiple Tenants, issuer identifier per Tenant
An issuer identifier, metadata document, and set of signing keys per Tenant

section.name: Choosing the OP Tenant
section.t: When one issuer identifier serves many OP Tenants, the RP has three ways to reach the Tenant it wants:

ul.li: tenant, when the RP knows the identifier. This is explicit, and takes precedence over anything else in the request.
domain_hint, when the RP only knows the user's domain. The OP resolves it, and may not resolve it to exactly one Tenant.
neither, leaving it to the OP. The OP can present a Tenant selector to the user, default to a Tenant for the client_id or the login_hint, or reject the request.

section.t: However the Tenant was reached, the ID Token carries the tenant claim, and the RP checks it against what it asked for.

section.name: An RP with many Tenants
section.t: The RP side mirrors the OP side. A SaaS application serving many customer organizations either registers a client_id per customer, or registers once and shares it.
A client_id per Tenant. aud names the RP Tenant, the way a per-Tenant issuer identifier names an OP Tenant.
This is what RPs do today when nothing else is available. It does not scale: every new customer is a new client registration, with its own credentials and lifecycle, for what is one application.

One client_id for all Tenants. The RP registers once, so aud is the same for every Tenant. The RP names the Tenant with the client_tenant request parameter, and the OP returns it in the aud_tenant claim.
The RP can register the Tenant identifiers it will use, so the OP can validate them and attach policy to them:

tr.td: One client_id, optionally with registered tenants

section.name: Telling the OP which RP Tenant
section.t: An RP that shares a client_id keeps track of its own Tenant across the authentication in one of three ways. Only the first is visible to the OP.

ul.li: client_tenant. The OP sees the RP Tenant, can apply policy for it such as access control, consent, or authentication method, and returns it in the aud_tenant claim.
state or session context. Common in practice, and invisible to the OP. The RP routes its own response, the OP has nothing to apply policy to, and no aud_tenant claim is returned.

A redirect_uri per Tenant. Also RP-side only. The OP treats the redirect_uri as opaque and does not parse a Tenant out of it. Deriving tenancy from a URL would make the redirection endpoint a protocol field, and would break the moment the RP changed its URL structure.

section.name: Naming the Account at the RP
section.t: The aud_sub claim is the RP's own identifier for the user, placed in the ID Token by the OP. It lets the OP refer to the user in terms the RP already uses, without the RP having to resolve sub first.

An aud_sub value is unique within the aud, across all of the RP's Tenants and not just within one. aud and aud_sub are therefore always enough to name the Account. An RP whose per-Tenant identifiers collide across Tenants, a per-Tenant sequential integer for example, constructs an aud_sub that does not collide, and keeps the construction to itself.
The aud_tenant and aud_sub claims are independent. The OP includes each one it knows:

tr.td: the OP knows the Account at the RP
the OP knows the RP Tenant
